sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (match the columns, true/false, fill in the blanks or one-word answers).

questions.q: Answer briefly: (i) Which activity can promote creative appreciation? (ii) How can children engage in creative movement?
questions.answer: (i) For example, drawing, painting, collage, clay modelling, decorating the classroom, nature walks. (ii) Through action rhymes, dancing and rhythmic movement — clapping, finger clicking and foot stamping to a beat.

questions.q: Answer in one sentence: (i) As an ECCE teacher, mention an activity you would organise for social skills in children of 1–3 years. (ii) Mention a cognitive skill that needs attention at the ECCE stage.
questions.answer: (i) For example, group play with a ball or blocks where children share and take turns, or singing action rhymes in a circle. (ii) Any one: memory, observation, classification, sequential thinking, problem solving, reasoning.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (i) ECCE teaching-learning strategies are essentially ________-centred. (ii) The teaching-learning approach should be ________, that is, including all children.
questions.answer: (i) child (ii) inclusive

questions.q: State True or False: (i) Print awareness is a part of emotional development. (ii) Changes in one domain can help or hinder development in another domain.
questions.answer: (i) False — it is part of language and emergent literacy. (ii) True.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (i) Play stimulates curiosity and ________. (ii) ________ strategies make children active participants rather than passive recipients in learning.
questions.answer: (i) exploration (ii) Play- and activity-based

questions.q: Answer in one word: (i) List any one pre-number concept. (ii) The movement of a child from egocentrism towards playing with and helping others.
questions.answer: (i) Any one: big–small, long–short, heavy–light, tall–short, thick–thin, wide–narrow, more–less, far–near. (ii) Socio-centrism (socialisation).

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Why are play and activity-based transactional strategies important for learning in children?
questions.answer: They give learning experiences in concrete form and make children active participants, not passive recipients. They nurture observation, experimentation, problem solving and creativity, and also promote physical, language and social development, fulfilling all developmental objectives.

questions.q: Describe any two major areas that need attention for cognitive development in children.
questions.answer: Sensory and perceptual development — plenty of activities for seeing, hearing, touch, smell and taste, since senses are the gateway of knowledge. Development of cognitive skills — memory, observation, classification, sequential thinking, problem solving and reasoning. (Also: formation of basic concepts, pre-number and environmental concepts.)

questions.q: Mention any four common activities for all-round development.
questions.answer: Any four: free and structured conversation, storytelling and story-making, dramatisation, rhymes and songs, music and movement, sand play, water play, puppet play, circle time, free indoor play with puzzles, beads and blocks, outdoor play, nature walks, field trips.

questions.q: What are creative activities? Give examples.
questions.answer: Activities that let children express themselves in their own way and develop imagination and aesthetic sense — drawing, colouring, painting, printing, tearing and pasting, collage, clay modelling, paper folding, creative movement, creative drama and make-believe play.

questions.q: List some ways of noting children's progress in an ECCE centre.
questions.answer: Regular observation of each child in all domains, daily records and diary notes, checklists of milestones, portfolios of children's work, and comparing with age norms; sharing these with parents.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: What do you mean by developmentally appropriate activities for different domains? Describe one such activity for toddlers.
questions.answer: Activities that match the children's age, developmental level, interests and needs in each domain — physical-motor, language, cognitive, socio-emotional and creative — challenging enough but not frustrating, and flexible for each child's pace. Example for toddlers (fine motor and cognitive): give large wooden beads of different colours and a thick string; children thread the beads, name colours and sort them into bowls. This builds eye-hand coordination, colour concepts and concentration.

or.q: Explain the pre-number concept. Describe an activity that can be used for cognitive development under the pre-number concept.
or.answer: Pre-number concepts are ideas of comparison that children must master before learning numbers: big–small (size), long–short (length), heavy–light (weight), tall–short (height), thick–thin, wide–narrow, more–less (quantity), far–near (distance). They help children judge the value of a number before learning mathematical operations, so they do not just memorise. Activity: give children sticks of different lengths and ask them to find the long and short ones, then arrange them from shortest to longest and say which is 'same as' another.

questions.q: Shama, an ECCE teacher, wants to facilitate creative and aesthetic development in children. Suggest activities.
questions.answer: Arts: drawing and colouring, painting, printing with leaves or vegetables, tearing and pasting, collage, clay modelling, paper folding. Creative movement: action rhymes, dancing, clapping and foot stamping to a beat. Creative drama: 'walk like an elephant', 'hop like a rabbit', dramatising stories with their own dialogues, dumb charades. Creative thinking: free and make-believe play, open-ended questions, making up stories and rhymes. Aesthetic appreciation: decorating the classroom, displays at eye level changed often, nature walks, beginning the day with songs. She should keep the atmosphere free, not authoritarian.

questions.q: Explain the role of an ECCE teacher in developing environmental concepts in children.
questions.answer: The immediate environment is natural (animals, birds, insects, plants, fruits, vegetables), physical (water, air, sky, earth, seasons, weather) and social (self and family, transport, community helpers, festivals). The teacher takes these up as projects or themes, uses nature walks, field trips, real objects, pictures and stories, encourages observation and questions, and introduces colour, number, shape, time and temperature through these themes.

questions.q: What are the major areas that need attention in language development at the ECCE stage?
questions.answer: Listening skills (sound discrimination, listening span, comprehension); vocabulary related to body, home and environment; speaking and oral expression (conversation, storytelling, dramatisation, puppets, picture reading); reading readiness (sound and visual discrimination, auditory-visual association, left-to-right direction); writing readiness (fine muscles, eye-hand coordination, letter perception). The home language should be the medium as far as possible.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Why should children be provided with ample fine motor and gross motor activities?
questions.answer: Motor development depends on neural and muscular maturation and on opportunities; it follows a fixed sequence but varies in rate. Gross motor activities — walking, balancing, running, jumping, climbing, swinging, throwing, catching, kicking — build strength, balance, coordination, stamina and health, give an outlet for energy and confidence in the body, and teach social skills such as taking turns on the swing. Fine motor activities — threading, tearing, cutting, pasting, colouring, painting, clay, paper folding, sorting, pouring — build control of eye, hand and finger muscles and eye-hand coordination. They lead to self-help skills (feeding, dressing, buttoning) and writing readiness, since formal writing needs strong, coordinated fingers. Because domains are interdependent, a physically active child also attends and participates better.

or.q: Explain why we say that development in all domains takes place in an integrated manner.
or.answer: Development in one domain influences the others, and deprivation in one affects all: a weak or listless child pays less attention, joins less and may become irritable. A single experience serves many domains — storytelling builds language, imagination, listening together and emotions; outdoor play builds motor skills and turn-taking and sharing. So the curriculum must be holistic, with balanced activities for all domains, observation of each child and partnership with parents.

questions.q: How does a child-centred approach influence teaching-learning strategies during the early years?
questions.answer: A child-centred approach puts the child's needs, interests, abilities and social context at the centre. So learning is play- and activity-based, with concrete, first-hand experiences in which children are active participants; activities follow the child's pace and short attention span and are flexible; the approach is inclusive so that every child feels safe and free from discrimination; uniformity and judgment are avoided; the home language is used; there is no formal teaching of the 3Rs; the teacher observes each child, builds a responsive relationship, plans developmentally appropriate activities across domains, and works with parents. Such strategies nurture observation, experimentation, problem solving and creativity along with physical, language and social development.
